newsitem.title: GREECE: Defeated Greek conservatives face "civil war".
newsitem.headline: Defeated Greek conservatives face "civil war".

text.p: Former Greek national economy minister Stephanos Manos, entering the ring for a bruising conservative leadership battle on Wednesday, blamed years of "civil war" in the party for two consecutive election defeats.
"For the past six years there has been a civil war being waged inside our party and this has cost us two elections. We need a leader to unite us," Manos told reporters.

The conservative New Democracy party was beaten by the ruling PASOK socialists in elections on Sunday, prompting party leader Miltiades Evert to resign. They have won only one of seven elections since 1981.
Manos, renowned for his blunt talk, was referring to a vicious personal feud between Evert and former prime minister Constantine Mitsotakis, who ruled from 1990 to 1993.
He was stating publicly what political commentators have asserted for years: Evert and Mitsotakis are tearing the party apart and ensuring that the socialists remain in power.
Mitsotakis, a provincial patriarch from Crete, blames Evert for his election defeat in October 1993 after rebel conservative deputies toppled his government.
Evert, a populist ex-Athens mayor known as "the Bulldozer", seized the conservative leadership after Mitsotakis's election loss. He accuses Mitsotakis of undermining him this time around.
So far the only declared candidates in the leadership race are Manos and Mitsotakis's daughter Dora Bakoyanni, a rising star and culture minister in her father's government.

Bakoyanni, 42, is a star performer in television debates or chat shows. She appeared to use the election campaign to promote herself as a future party leader and to build her popular image, with thousands of posters billing her simply as "Dora".
Her candidacy is seen by Evert supporters as a back-door way for her father to regain a hold on the party machine.
Many conservative deputies have asked Evert to change his mind and run again for the leadership but Mitsotakis, a powerful backbencher, has threatened to run himself if that happens.
"The danger of a split is obvious," Andreas Andrianopoulos, a former conservative industry minister said.
Manos said that apart from the Evert-Mitsotakis personality clash, the party lost because it had no clear ideology.
"Instead of telling voters that New Democracy will cut down on the unproductive state and move on with brave privatisations, we flirt with socialist beliefs. This is crazy," he said.
Manos is an avowed neo-liberal who tried, and failed, to privatise aggressively as Mitsotakis's third and final economy minister.
Evert is closer to Constantine Karamanlis, who founded New Democracy in 1974 and believed the state must have a strong role in the economy.
"Everything will be known by next week but it is clear that Mitsotakis and Evert can no longer co-exist in New Democracy," one official said.
